propositions.text: The Applicants are Ms. Oluchi Theresa Nonso-Ajah, her husband Mr. Kingsley Nonso Ajah and their eight-year-old son Josiah Uchechukwu Kingsley Ajah.
propositions.quote: The Applicants are Ms. Oluchi Theresa Nonso-Ajah, her husband Mr. Kingsley Nonso Ajah and their eight-year-old son Josiah Uchechukwu Kingsley Ajah.

propositions.text: The couple are citizens of Nigeria and their son is a citizen of the U.S.A.
propositions.quote: The couple are citizens of Nigeria and their son is a citizen of the U.S.A.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicants' identities and citizenships: Nigerian couple and their U.S. citizen son.

propositions.text: The Applicants entered Canada in fall 2016 and made refugee claims based on Ms. Nonso-Ajah's fear after refusing to be Chief Priestess.
propositions.quote: The Applicants entered Canada in the fall of 2016 and made refugee claims, based on Ms. Nonso-Ajah’s fear of her community after she refused to become the Chief Priestess.

propositions.text: The RPD rejected their claim in 2018, excluding Mr. Nonso Ajah under Article 1F(b) and finding internal flight alternative for Ms. Nonso-Ajah and son.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Protection Division [RPD] rejected their claim in 2018, finding that Mr. Nonso Ajah was excluded pursuant to Article 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention and that Ms. Nonso-Ajah and her son had a viable internal flight alternative in Abuja.

propositions.text: The RAD rejected their appeal in 2020.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Appeal Division [RAD] rejected their appeal in 2020.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts the Applicants' refugee claim history and rejections by RPD and RAD.

propositions.text: The couple had two more children in Canada in 2017 and 2019 and were expecting another child at the H&C application time.
propositions.quote: The couple had two more children while in Canada, in 2017 and 2019. At the time of their H&C application, they were expecting another child.

propositions.text: Their oldest child attends school in Canada.
propositions.quote: Their oldest child, the minor Applicant, attends school in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the couple's additional children born in Canada and their oldest child's schooling.

propositions.text: Before Canada, Mr. Nonso Ajah worked internationally; Ms. Nonso-Ajah stayed mostly in Nigeria and earned a bachelor's in economics.
propositions.quote: Before coming to Canada, Mr. Nonso Ajah worked in various parts of the world, including Brazil and South Africa, while Ms. Nonso-Ajah stayed in Nigeria for the most part where she obtained a bachelor’s degree in economics.

propositions.text: In Canada, both worked as warehouse associates at Amazon, upgraded education and skills, and Ms. Nonso-Ajah worked as a casual temporary resident support aid for seniors.
propositions.quote: Since coming to Canada, the couple have both been employed as warehouse associates at Amazon. They have both upgraded their education and skills. In addition, Ms. Nonso-Ajah has been working as a casual temporary resident support aid for seniors.

propositions.text: They volunteer at their church and help elderly in their community.
propositions.quote: The couple also volunteer at their church and help the elderly in their community.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the Applicants' prior work, education, employment, and community involvement in Canada.

propositions.text: Mr. Nonso Ajah has medical conditions including pulmonary sarcoidosis, Type 2 diabetes, liver and blood pressure concerns, and receives ongoing treatment.
propositions.quote: Mr. Nonso Ajah suffers from several medical conditions, including pulmonary sarcoidosis, Type 2 diabetes, and concerns related to his liver and blood pressure. He receives ongoing medical treatment and takes various medications to manage his conditions.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Nonso Ajah's medical conditions and ongoing treatment.

propositions.text: Applicants applied for permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate grounds under s. 25(1) IRPA, refused May 31, 2021 by Senior Officer.
propositions.quote: The Applicants applied for permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate grounds [H&C application] under s. 25(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA]. The H&C Application was refused on May 31, 2021 [Decision] by a Senior Officer of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada [Officer].

propositions.text: Applicants seek judicial review of the refusal of their H&C application.
propositions.quote: The Applicants seek judicial review of the refusal of their H&C application.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Applicants' H&C application refusal and their judicial review seeking.

propositions.text: I grant the application because the Officer erred in assessing establishment and country conditions, especially medical treatment evidence for Mr. Nonso Ajah.
propositions.quote: I grant the application as I find the Officer erred with respect to their assessment of the Applicants’ establishment and the country conditions evidence, most notably the evidence concerning available medical treatment for Mr. Nonso Ajah in Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: The court grants the application, finding errors in the Officer's assessment of establishment and country conditions evidence.

propositions.text: Applicants argue Officer erred in assessing (1) establishment, (2) hardship in Nigeria, and (3) best interests of children.
propositions.quote: The Applicants argue that the Officer erred in assessing (1) establishment, (2) hardship in Nigeria, and (3) the best interests of the children.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicants argue the Officer erred on establishment, hardship, and children's best interests assessments.

propositions.text: Both parties agree issues are reviewable on reasonableness standard per Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65.
propositions.quote: Both parties agree that the issues are reviewable on the reasonableness standard (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov]).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes both parties agree on reasonableness standard of review per Vavilov.

propositions.text: A reasonable decision is internally coherent, rational, and justified by facts and law: Vavilov para 85.
propositions.quote: A reasonable decision “is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker”: Vavilov, at para 85.

propositions.text: Applicant bears onus to show decision unreasonable: Vavilov para 100.
propositions.quote: The onus is on the Applicant to demonstrate that the decision is unreasonable: Vavilov, at para 100.

propositions.text: To set aside decision, court must find serious shortcomings undermining justification, intelligibility, transparency: Vavilov para 100.
propositions.quote: To set aside a decision on this basis, “the reviewing court must be satisfied that there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency”: Vavilov, at para 100.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the reasonableness standard and burden per Vavilov.

propositions.text: Decision focuses on Officer's assessment of establishment and findings on hardship from adverse country conditions.
propositions.quote: My decision will focus on two issues: the Officer’s assessment of the Applicants’ establishment, and the Officer’s findings on hardship arising from adverse country conditions.

paragraphs.summary: The court states it will focus on establishment and hardship issues in its decision.

propositions.text: Applicants submitted evidence of establishment including employment, tax, bank statements, and 14 support letters from community and MP.
propositions.quote: In support of their H&C application, the Applicants submitted evidence about their establishment in Canada including their employment records, tax filing, bank statements, and the like. They also submitted 14 support letters from friends, landlord, community organizations, and a local Member of Parliament attesting to their establishment and ties in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicants submitted extensive evidence of establishment including documents and support letters.

propositions.text: Officer gave establishment 'some weight' noting employment and community activity but found it not 'exceptional' compared to similar individuals.
propositions.quote: The Officer gave their establishment “some weight”, noting that the Applicants are employed and are active in the community. However, the Officer found that their establishment was not “exceptional in relation to similarly situated individuals who have been in Canada for a comparable amount of time.”

paragraphs.summary: The Officer gave some weight to establishment but found it not exceptional compared to peers.

propositions.text: Applicants argue Officer set an impossible high threshold requiring exceptional establishment.
propositions.quote: The Applicants argue that the Officer set a high and impossible threshold by requiring them to demonstrate an exceptional level of establishment.

propositions.text: Applicants say they showed exemplary commitment to integration, employment, financial stability, credit score, and friendships.
propositions.quote: In the Applicants’ view, they have shown “exemplary commitment towards a speedy integration and becoming self-supporting”, in addition to raising their children. They highlight their employment, financial stability, credit score, and friendships.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue the Officer unreasonably required exceptional establishment despite their strong integration evidence.

propositions.text: Applicants argue it is unreasonable to require 'extraordinary' establishment without explanation, citing Sivalingam, Apura, Damian cases.
propositions.quote: The Applicants argue “it is unreasonable to require, without more explanation, an “extraordinary” level of establishment”: Sivalingam v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 1185 [Sivalingam] at para 13; Apura v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 762 at para 23; and Damian v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 1158 [Damian] at para 21.

propositions.text: Applicants say Officer failed to explain what evidence would show exceptional establishment and why their evidence deserved more weight.
propositions.quote: They argue that the Officer gave no indication of what other evidence would show “exceptional” establishment and failed to explain why all of the evidence did not warrant more weight.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue the Officer unreasonably required extraordinary establishment and failed to explain weight of evidence.

propositions.text: Respondent submits Officer reasonably considered Applicants' efforts and gave some weight to establishment.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the Officer reasonably considered the Applicant’s circumstances (including their efforts to work, upgrade their skills and their community involvement) and gave their establishment some weight.

propositions.text: Respondent says Officer justified conclusion that evidence did not show integration causing hardship beyond control or IRPA anticipation.
propositions.quote: In the Respondent’s view, the Officer justified their ultimate conclusion on establishment based on the evidence, which did “not support that they have integrated into Canadian society to the extent that their departure would cause hardship that was beyond their control and not anticipated by the IRPA.”

propositions.text: Respondent argues disagreement with weight given is insufficient to overturn the Decision.
propositions.quote: The Respondent argues that a disagreement with the weight given by the Officer to certain factors is insufficient to overturn the Decision.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues Officer reasonably assessed establishment and weight disagreement is insufficient to overturn.

propositions.text: Respondent argues Officer did not require 'exceptional' establishment but used term descriptively.
propositions.quote: The Respondent also argues that the Officer did not require the Applicants to demonstrate “exceptional” establishment—rather, this term was used as a descriptor.

propositions.text: Respondent cites Davis v Canada and Lopez Segura to say use of 'exceptional' word alone is not proof of unreasonableness.
propositions.quote: In the Respondent’s view, the Officer’s reasons were similar to those upheld by Justice Favel in Davis v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 238: [43] The mere use of the word “exceptional” is not proof that the Officer applied an unreasonably high threshold. As was stated in Lopez Segura v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2009 FC 894 at paragraph 29, “[i]t is not the use of particular words that is determinative; it is whether it can be said on a reading of the decision as a whole that the officer applied the correct test and conducted a proper analysis.”

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues 'exceptional' was descriptive, not a high threshold, citing case law.

propositions.text: Respondent cites Huang and related cases supporting Officer's approach.
propositions.quote: The Respondent also cites Chief Justice Crampton’s decision in Huang v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 265 [Huang] at paras 19-20 and several cases following it including Al-Abayechi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 1280 at para 14.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent cites Huang and related cases supporting Officer's approach.

propositions.text: Distinction exists between showing exceptional misfortunes (consistent with H&C purpose) and requiring exceptional establishment (artificial standard).
propositions.quote: A distinction must be drawn, in my view, between demonstrating “the existence of misfortunes or other circumstances that are exceptional” (Huang, at para 20) on the one hand, and achieving an “exceptional” degree of establishment, on the other.

propositions.text: H&C provisions aim to relieve misfortunes that excite reasonable desire for relief (Kanthasamy, Chirwa).
propositions.quote: The former analysis is consistent with the core purpose of the H&C provisions under IRPA to offer equitable relief in circumstances that “would excite in a reasonable [person] in a civilized community a desire to relieve the misfortunes of another”: Kanthasamy v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61 at para 21, citing Chirwa v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) (1970), 4 IAC 338 at 350.

propositions.text: Requiring exceptional establishment sets an artificial standard for positive H&C outcome.
propositions.quote: The latter approach, in contrast, sets an artificial standard for establishment against which individual applicants are measured in order to obtain a positive H&C outcome.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds requiring exceptional establishment is an artificial standard inconsistent with H&C's purpose to relieve misfortunes.

propositions.text: Justice Zinn in Zhang distinguishes between relief for exceptional personal circumstances and requiring exceptional misfortunes relative to others.
propositions.quote: In appreciating the difference between the two approaches, I find instructive, the following quote from Justice Zinn in Zhang v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 1482 [Zhang]: [23] There is a significant difference between observing that this exceptional relief is provided for because the personal circumstances of some are such that deportation falls with more force on them than others, and stating that the relief is available only to those who demonstrate the existence of misfortunes or other circumstances that are exceptional relative to others.

propositions.text: The first explains why exemption exists; the second wrongly adds a condition to the exception (Zhang).
propositions.quote: The first explains why the exemption is there, while the second purports to identify those who may benefit from the exemption. The second imports a condition into the exception that is not there. [Emphasis in original]

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Zhang to explain the difference between relief rationale and improper condition requiring exceptional misfortunes.

propositions.text: The issue is whether the Applicants' circumstances, including establishment, warrant equitable relief on H&C grounds.
propositions.quote: the issue is not so much whether the Applicants’ establishment is “exceptional” or not, but whether the particular circumstances of the case, including the Applicants’ establishment, are such that it would warrant a granting of the equitable relief on H&C grounds.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue is whether the Applicants' circumstances, including establishment, warrant equitable relief on H&C grounds.

propositions.text: Analyzing the officer's reasons as a whole will determine if 'exceptional' creates a higher threshold than subsection 25(1) IRPA.
propositions.quote: An analysis of the officer’s reasons, considered as a whole, will help determine whether the use of the word “exceptional” creates a higher threshold than that provided for in subsection 25(1) of the IRPA

paragraphs.summary: The court will analyze the officer's reasons to see if 'exceptional' sets a higher threshold than subsection 25(1) IRPA.

propositions.text: The Officer's use of 'exceptional' imported an additional legal standard into the H&C analysis.
propositions.quote: I find the Officer’s use of the word “exceptional” was not merely used descriptively, but instead imported an additional legal standard into the H&C analysis

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer's use of 'exceptional' imposed an additional legal standard in the H&C analysis.

propositions.text: The Officer applied an exceptionality assessment to the Applicants' establishment compared to others, not to the overall H&C relief.
propositions.quote: This signals the Officer was applying an exceptionality assessment in relation to the Applicants’ establishment, and not in relation to whether the Applicants’ circumstances, taken as whole, would warrant the granting of the exceptional H&C relief.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer assessed exceptionality of establishment compared to others, not overall H&C relief.

propositions.text: The Officer erred by not explaining why the Applicants' evidence did not show integration causing hardship beyond control and why establishment was not exceptional.
propositions.quote: The Officer erred by concluding, without explaining, why the Applicants’ evidence did not show that “they have integrated into Canadian society to the extent that their departure would cause hardship that was beyond their control”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer erred by failing to explain why Applicants' evidence did not show integration causing hardship or exceptional establishment.

propositions.text: The Officer's unexplained conclusion was unreasonable given evidence of employment, church involvement, and elderly support.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s conclusion, in the absence of an explanation, was unreasonable given the amount of evidence before the Officer, not only about the adult Applicants’ employment but also about involvement in their church and support for the elderly.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer's unexplained conclusion unreasonable given evidence of employment, church involvement, and support for elderly.

propositions.text: This case differs from cited cases because Applicants provided personalized evidence which the Officer failed to consider, amounting to reviewable error.
propositions.quote: the Officer’s failure to consider such evidence, or engage in a meaningful analysis of such evidence amounted to a reviewable error.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds this case differs from cited cases as Applicants provided personalized evidence ignored by the Officer, a reviewable error.

propositions.text: The Officer found Applicants did not provide enough info on threats and could relocate; gave adverse country conditions little weight.
propositions.quote: The Officer found that the Applicants had not provided more information on threats stemming from Ms. Nonso-Ajah’s refusal to become Chief Priestess, and that the family could relocate within Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found Applicants lacked info on threats and could relocate; gave adverse country conditions little weight.

propositions.text: The court rejects Applicants' argument that Officer applied higher risk threshold and ignored insecurity and regional differences.
propositions.quote: I do not find persuasive the Applicant’s arguments that the Officer erred by incorrectly applying the higher threshold associated with proving risk, instead of the lower evidentiary threshold associated with hardship

propositions.text: Applicants partially relied on refused refugee claim ground and failed to show hardship persists after five years; some arguments were raised late.
propositions.quote: Applicants’ H&C submission was partially relying on the same ground as their refused refugee claim but failed to adduce evidence why, five years hence, hardship still exists. I also note that much of the Applicants’ arguments before this Court in this respect were not advanced in the H&C submission and were thus inappropriately raised.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects Applicants' arguments on risk threshold and insecurity, noting partial reliance on refused refugee claim and late arguments.

propositions.text: The court finds merit in Applicants' argument that Officer ignored evidence on medical treatment accessibility in Nigeria.
propositions.quote: I find merit in the Applicant’s argument that the Officer ignored evidence, including evidence from the National Documentation Package [NDP] indicating that treatment for Mr. Nonso Ajah’s medical conditions may not be accessible in Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds merit in Applicants' argument that Officer ignored evidence on medical treatment accessibility in Nigeria.

propositions.text: Applicants submitted extensive medical documentation of Mr. Nonso Ajah's conditions and treatments in Canada.
propositions.quote: The Applicants submitted voluminous medical documentation showing Mr. Nonso Ajah’s frequent visits to hospitals, medical clinics and specialists in Canada and various assessments performed on him

paragraphs.summary: Applicants submitted extensive medical documentation of Mr. Nonso Ajah's conditions and treatments in Canada.

propositions.text: Applicants compiled a list from NDP showing some prescribed drugs are unavailable or lack alternatives in Nigeria.
propositions.quote: According to the list, some of the drugs that the Applicant has been prescribed in Canada are not available in Nigeria, nor is there any alternative available.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants compiled NDP-based list showing some prescribed drugs unavailable or lacking alternatives in Nigeria.

propositions.text: Applicants included UK Home Office report stating diabetes treatment is insufficient and inaccessible in many Nigerian regions.
propositions.quote: There is no specific Institution designated to treat diabetes in Nigeria…available human resources and infrastructures are grossly insufficient for the country…

paragraphs.summary: Applicants included UK report stating diabetes treatment is insufficient and inaccessible in many Nigerian regions.

propositions.text: Applicants argue Officer ignored objective country conditions and contradicted himself on medication cost and employment challenges.
propositions.quote: The Applicants submitted that the Officer ignored the objective country conditions with regard to healthcare in Nigeria. Further, the Officer stated that while medications may be expensive in Nigeria, the Applicants are also paying for their medications in Canada, This, the Applicant submits, directly contradicted the Officer’s acknowledgment that finding a job may be challenging for the Applicants

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue Officer ignored country conditions and contradicted himself on medication cost and employment challenges.

propositions.text: The court accepts part of the Applicants' argument regarding the Officer's assessment.
propositions.quote: I accept part of the Applicant’s argument.

paragraphs.summary: The court accepts part of the Applicants' argument regarding the Officer's assessment.

propositions.text: The Officer found most medications available or with alternatives in Nigeria; financial burden could be eased by employment; no medical evidence that Mr. Ajah cannot work.
propositions.quote: The submissions show that [Mr. Nonso Ajah]’s medical conditions are being managed through medications. The submissions also show that most of the medications [Mr. Nonso Ajah] is taking are available in Nigeria and most of the ones that are not available, have suitable alternatives available.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer found most medications available or with alternatives; financial burden could be eased by employment; no medical evidence Mr. Ajah cannot work.

propositions.text: The Officer did not contradict on ability to pay; considering employment and skills to assess ability to pay was open and proper.
propositions.quote: I find the Officer did not make any contradictory finding, as the Applicants submitted. I also agree with the Respondent that it was open to the Officer to consider the Applicants’ employment and skills in assessing their ability to secure employment in Nigeria and pay for medication

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer did not contradict on ability to pay and properly considered employment and skills.

propositions.text: The Officer's conclusion on hardship from healthcare conditions was unreasonable as some medications are unavailable in Nigeria.
propositions.quote: I do find unreasonable the Officer’s conclusion with respect to the hardship caused by adverse country conditions in relation to available health care. As noted above, and as the Officer acknowledged, not all of the medications that Mr. Nonso Ajah requires are available in Nigeria.

propositions.text: Focusing on ability to pay and ignoring medication availability evidence was an error by the Officer.
propositions.quote: By focusing on the Applicants’ ability to pay, and ignoring the country conditions evidence regarding the availability of the medications, I find the Officer erred.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer's conclusion on healthcare hardship unreasonable and that ignoring medication availability evidence was an error.

propositions.text: Respondent argues Applicants bore onus to show medications unavailable, citing Adedeji case where evidence was lacking.
propositions.quote: The Respondent argues that the onus was on the Applicants to show that the medications are not available in Nigeria, similar to Adedeji v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 291

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues Applicants bore onus to show medications unavailable, citing Adedeji case.

propositions.text: The court finds Adedeji inapplicable; adverse country condition evidence can come from various sources including NDP documents.
propositions.quote: Adedeji, in my view, is not applicable. I note, first of all, adverse country condition evidence can come in different forms. It is not restricted only to evidence “from the relevant health authorities” in the home country.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Adedeji inapplicable; adverse country condition evidence can come from various sources including NDP.

propositions.text: Applicants submitted relevant health care evidence including medical records, drug list, and country condition reports.
propositions.quote: the Applicants did submit relevant health care evidence including Mr. Nonso Ajah’s medical records, the list of drugs he relies on, and the NDP country condition reports regarding the availability of the medications.

propositions.text: Officer concluded adverse country conditions did not cause hardship despite serious health issues and evidence.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s conclusion that the existence of such adverse country conditions did not give rise to hardship

propositions.text: Officer's conclusion lacks transparency, intelligibility and justification and must be set aside.
propositions.quote: lacks transparency, intelligibility and justification and must be set aside.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants submitted health evidence; Officer found no hardship; court finds Officer's conclusion unjustified and sets it aside.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is granted.
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is granted.

paragraphs.summary: Court grants the application for judicial review.

propositions.text: No question for certification.
propositions.quote: There is no question for certification.

propositions.text: Judgment: application for judicial review granted; matter sent back for redetermination by different officer.
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is granted and the matter sent back for redetermination by a different officer.

paragraphs.summary: Court grants review, sends matter back for redetermination, and finds no question for certification.
